title: Ibn Khaldun on teaching
tomorrow: how do you describe a view you disagree with, fairly?

cards: A coach who screams, a tutor who sighs every time you get it wrong. Some of us still flinch at the memory. What happens to a student who's taught with harshness?
Ibn Khaldun gave it a short chapter in the Muqaddimah, and its title gives the answer away: severity toward students does them harm.

teach.b: Students raised with force and compulsion, he writes, are crushed by it. They lose their energy, grow lazy, and learn to lie and pretend, to escape the hand raised over them.

He records a caliph's advice to his son's teacher, from Harun al-Rashid: don't be so strict that you kill his mind, nor so soft that he gets used to idleness; correct him with kindness and gentleness as far as you can, and only then with firmness.
That's the word for today, lightly: teach gently. And it gathers the week. Hasan al-Basri's shepherd: the shepherd's care.
Ibn Battuta at the edge of Tangier: alone, on the road. His Fridays in white: Friday in Mali. Ibn Jubayr's lamps and water: a pilgrim's journal.
Ibn Fadlan's frozen beard: the far north. Ibn Khaldun's 'asabiyya: solidarity holds.

teach.h: A WEEK OF CARRYING EACH OTHER.
teach.b: The thread: every one is about how people carry each other, a flock, a family left behind, a congregation, a group, a student.

In a hadith in al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says God is gentle and loves gentleness in all things. A week of travelers and rulers ends at a small desk, with a kid and a pencil.

how: Muslim teachers and parents cite Ibn Khaldun's chapter and the hadith on gentleness when they talk about raising and teaching children with kindness.

games.q: what does “ibn khaldun on teaching” mean?
o: his list of subjects a student should master first
his warning that harshness in teaching harms students
his rules for how long a school day should last

games.q: the chapter, and the week — tap the pairs.

s: Ibn Khaldun says strictness makes students work harder and better
he says harshness makes them lazy, and teaches them to lie and pretend.
he records advice not to be so soft that a student grows idle
kindness first, firmness only when needed.
a hadith in al-Bukhari says God loves gentleness in all things
God is gentle and loves gentleness.

games.q: your little brother keeps missing the same math problem, and you're about to snap. what fits Ibn Khaldun?
o: slow down and try a kinder way of explaining it.
raise your voice once so he knows it matters.
do the problem for him so nobody gets upset.
games.why: harshness, he says, makes a student shut down and hide. kindness comes first, and doing it for him isn't teaching.

practice: Think of someone you'll teach or explain something to soon: a kid, a coworker, a parent with a new phone. Wish: what you want them to learn. Obstacle: the moment you're likely to get impatient.
Plan: when that moment comes, slow down and say it a gentler way.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Khaldun on teaching: his chapter warning that harshness harms students, and counseling kindness first.

orig.note: Arabic: al-rifq, gentleness, the word in the hadith that God loves gentleness.

carryVoice: For the week: teach gently, kindness first and firmness only after. That's a week, carried.

sources.ref: Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah, chapter 6 (severity to students does them harm; Harun al-Rashid's instructions to his son's teacher)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6927 (God is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters)
